claims.text: Replacing a fixed EAM reference with an adaptive, actively learned NNIP trained on solid and liquid ab initio configurations near melting will improve reference–target phase-space overlap.
The target materials are multicomponent high-entropy alloys in equilibrium at high temperatures, with both solid and liquid states considered.
An on-the-fly active-learning scheme can develop an NNIP incorporating representative ab initio liquid configurations for use as a thermodynamic-integration reference.
The proposed method applies to equimolar or near-equimolar quinary-or-higher high-entropy alloys.
The applicable temperature range is approximately within ±10% of the alloy melting temperature.
Within the proposed temperature range, solid and liquid configurations coexist or are accessible.
The flexible functional form of an NNIP can capture a broader spectrum of atomic configurations, including disordered liquid-like states, than EAM potentials.
Training on diverse ab initio configurations that include high-temperature liquids produces a smoother and more continuous free-energy landscape.
The smoother NNIP landscape reduces mismatch along the thermodynamic-integration path.
Improved reference–target overlap makes thermodynamic integration more accurate and efficient than integration using conventional EAM-based TOR-TILD references.
The NNIP reference is expected to reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 30–50% relative to TOR-TILD's EAM references.
The NNIP-based free-energy estimates are expected to agree with full ab initio molecular-dynamics benchmarks to within approximately 5 meV/atom.
Current EAM-based TOR-TILD references exhibit significant integration-path mismatches because EAM lacks sufficient configurational flexibility to represent ab initio liquid states.
The intervention should be most effective for high-entropy alloys with complex multicomponent chemistries near their melting points.
The method's utility for simpler systems or substantially undercooled liquids is uncertain.
A comparison against standard EAM-based TOR-TILD and fully converged ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy calculations can test the NNIP-reference method.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement, at least a 30% mismatch reduction, or accuracy within approximately 5 meV/atom would falsify the hypothesis.
